posts.title: What my rescue cat taught me about patience
posts.excerpt: She hid under the bed for eleven days. Here is why that was exactly the right pace.
body: When I brought Milo home from the shelter, the woman at the desk warned me: give her time. I nodded and thought, sure, a day or two. She spent eleven days under my bed.
I could see one paw from where I sat on the floor. That was the whole relationship for a while. One paw, occasionally withdrawn.
## Patience is a skill pets teach better than people do

Everything in me wanted to reach in, pull her out, hold her, show her the good life. But cats do not work that way. Trust is not something you can hand over. It has to be left on the floor, near the bed, like a treat at 2am that disappears by morning.
So I stopped reaching. I sat in the same spot each evening and read aloud, badly, whatever book was nearby. She never came out. I kept going anyway.

On day twelve she came out while I was making tea. Just to watch. On day fourteen she ate while I was in the room. By the third week she was sleeping on the chair next to me, and by the second month she had claimed my laptop as a heated bed.
## What this has to do with work

I run a pet products company now, and people are surprised when I say the best part of the job is still this: learning that animals set the pace. You cannot rush a cat out from under a bed, and you cannot rush a design into being good either. You test, you wait, you adjust.
Milo tests every product that comes through our office. The ones she ignores go back to the drawing board. The ones she sleeps on, we ship.
If you have just adopted a shy cat, my only advice is this: sit on the floor, read something out loud, and count the days in paws, not hours.

posts.title: The first night home with a new puppy
posts.excerpt: Nobody sleeps. That is normal. A few things that made night two easier than night one.
body: The drive home was perfect. The puppy slept in my daughter's lap the whole way, and we had already picked a name. Then the sun went down.
At 1am the whining started. By 2am it was crying, and at 3am my wife said the thing every new puppy owner says: are we sure about this?
## Why the first night is so hard

Your puppy has never slept alone. For eight weeks, home has been a warm pile of siblings and a mother that smelled like breakfast. Your living room, however nice, is a strange cave with no pile in it.
The crying is not misbehavior. It is a very small animal calling for its family, and you are now the family.
## Three things that helped on night two
First, we moved the crate next to our bed. Close enough that a finger hanging down counted as company.
Second, a ticking clock wrapped in a towel under the blanket. It sounds silly until you remember the heartbeat argument: it worked within an hour.
Third, a toy from the breeder that smelled like the litter. Scent does more work than any gadget.
Night three was quiet. Night four, he slept through. Within two weeks the crate was his den and he walked in on his own when he was tired.

I think about that first night a lot, because at Poteho we design bedding for exactly this moment. A bed a puppy can dig into, with walls that touch its back, does more for sleep than any expensive thing we could add. The puppy does not need luxury. It needs something that feels like the pile it left behind.

posts.title: Why dogs follow you everywhere
posts.excerpt: Bathroom door closed, dog outside it. Always. There is a reason, and it is mostly flattering.
body: Every dog owner knows the shadow. You stand up, the dog stands up. You go to the kitchen, the dog is in the kitchen. You close the bathroom door and a nose appears under it like a periscope.
People joke that their dog has no concept of privacy. The truth is sweeter than that.
## You are the pack
Dogs are descended from animals that survived by staying together. Separation from the group once meant danger, so the instinct to keep the group in sight runs deep. In your house, the group is you.
Following you is not neediness in the human sense. It is your dog doing the oldest job it has: keeping the pack together and keeping an eye on its favorite member.

There is also the boring answer, which is that good things happen where you are. Food appears, doors open, walks begin. From your dog's point of view, you are the source of all major events. Of course they track you.
## When following is worth a closer look

Most of the time this is harmless and even endearing. But if the following is sudden, or comes with whining at any distance, pacing, or a dog that cannot settle in a room alone, it can tip into real separation anxiety.
The fix is not to push the dog away. It is to make alone time boring-but-safe: a stuffed toy in another room, short separations that always end well, and no big farewells at the door.

Our office dog, a beagle named Bao, follows the production manager on her entire morning rounds. When we test a new leash or harness sample, Bao's willingness to trot off happily at the end of it tells us more than any spec sheet. A dog that feels secure walks loose. A dog that does not, checks back every few steps.
So next time the bathroom door will not shut properly because of a snout, take it as the compliment it is.

posts.title: Do cats really get lonely?
posts.excerpt: The independent cat is partly myth. Here is what to watch for if yours spends long days alone.
body: Cats have a reputation for being fine alone. Some are. But after years of watching cats, and after hearing the same story from hundreds of owners, I would put it differently: cats get lonely quietly, and they hide it well.
## The myth of the totally independent cat

Feral cats live in colonies. Mother cats co-raise kittens. In a barn, cats sleep in heaps. The independent house cat is a fairly recent invention, and a lot of them are not as independent as we assume.

The problem is that loneliness in cats does not look like loneliness in dogs. A lonely dog makes noise and eats your shoes. A lonely cat just... flattens. It sleeps more, plays less, grooms too much or not enough, and greets you with less of the usual commentary.
## Signs worth taking seriously

Watch for changes rather than single symptoms. A cat that used to meet you at the door and now does not. A cat that over-grooms a bare patch on its belly. A cat that eats from boredom and one that stops bothering, both count.
Long empty days are the usual cause. Two income households, long commutes, travel. The cat is not sad in a dramatic way. It is just under-stimulated, and months of under-stimulation add up.
## What actually helps

Window view, climbing space, and a predictable play session when you get home. Puzzle feeders so the day has structure. If the budget and the cat allow it, a second cat with a careful, slow introduction.

This is a big part of why our design work starts with how a cat spends a solo day. A window perch at the right height, a scratcher it will actually use, toys that move like prey instead of like plastic. None of it replaces you. All of it makes the alone hours better.
Cats do not ask for company loudly. They just do better when it is there.

posts.title: Winter walks are the best walks (yes, really)
posts.excerpt: Cold mornings, empty streets, a dog that finally gets to use its nose. Winter deserves a second look.
body: Somewhere around the second week of December, every year, a certain kind of dog owner decides walks are a summer activity and the yard will do. I used to be that owner. Then I got a dog who disagreed, loudly, at 6:40 every morning.
## What winter gives you

Empty streets, for one. In summer the park is chaos of strollers and scooters. In winter you get the whole place, and a dog on a quiet trail sniffing frost is a different animal than the same dog navigating summer crowds.

Cold also sharpens scent. Many dogs are simply more engaged in cold air. Mine will spend ten minutes on one frozen grass patch, reading the neighborhood news, while in August he gives it a two-second glance and moves on.
## The gear part, briefly
You do not need much. Paws are the weak point for most dogs, not the body. Salt and ice are the actual enemies: they sting, they crack pads, and city salt is mildly toxic when licked off.

A thin paw wax or a simple bootie solves most of it. Short-coated dogs, seniors, and small breeds often do want a jacket. Watch the dog, not the thermometer. Shivering, paw-lifting, and a hunched back mean it is time to head home.

For reflective gear, winter is when it earns its price. Dark mornings and dark evenings mean your dog is far less visible than you think. A stitch of reflective thread on a harness catches headlights from much further away than a bright color does. We learned this the hard way in our early samples and now it is a standard detail on everything we make for winter markets.
Give winter walks one honest try. Pick the coldest, clearest morning you can, take a thermos, and let the dog set the pace. You might find, as I did, that it becomes the best part of the day.

posts.title: Choosing a carrier your cat won't hate
posts.excerpt: If the carrier only comes out for the vet, your cat has already made up its mind about it.
body: Ask a cat owner about carrier day and you will hear the same story. The carrier comes out of the closet, the cat vanishes, and twenty minutes later there is a person with a scratched arm chasing a small angry cloud around the apartment.
It does not have to be like this.
## The real problem is not the carrier

The problem is what the carrier means. It appears twice a year, always before something unpleasant, and it always ends at a place with clipper smells and dog noises. Your cat is not afraid of the box. It is afraid of the schedule.

So the fix starts weeks before any vet trip: the carrier becomes furniture. Sit it in the living room, door open, blanket inside, treats appearing in it at random. When the carrier is just the cozy box that sometimes dispenses chicken, vet day becomes a normal event in a familiar space.
## Features that actually matter
Top loading is the feature I would not give up. A frightened cat can be lowered in gently instead of pushed into a front hatch it is actively defending.

Beyond that: a solid frame that does not sag when lifted, mesh panels for airflow and view, secure latches, and a pad you can remove and wash. Size should let the cat stand and turn, not host a party.
## What we learned testing carriers

We tested a whole range before adding one to our line, and the results humbled us. Cats preferred carriers with a dark interior and one small window over the airy, bright designs the humans in the room liked best. The lesson stuck: we design for the animal, and the human gets a handle they like and a washable pad.

If your cat already hates its carrier, do not throw it out. Leave it out for a month with the door open and feed near it, then in it. Fear fades when the object stops predicting bad days. Give it time. Cats are fair, once you speak their language.

posts.title: How long can you leave a dog alone? An honest answer
posts.excerpt: Not the answer you will find on posters. The honest one depends on the dog, the day, and what you do about it.
body: There is a number that gets passed around: four hours. Some say six. Some say a dog is fine all day if it has a yard. Most of these answers come from people selling something, so let me try to be honest instead.
## The honest answer

It depends on the dog, and the range is wide. A mature, settled adult of a calmer breed can handle a full workday better than most people expect, if its needs are met before and after. A young puppy cannot. An hour or two at a time is the realistic limit for a puppy under six months, because their bladder and their brain are both unfinished.
Breed matters but individual history matters more. A rescue that spent a year alone in a yard may fall apart at thirty minutes. A confident two-year-old Lab may yawn at eight hours occasionally.
## What ruins a workday for a dog
It is rarely the length alone. It is the sameness. Eight hours of nothing is the problem, not eight hours as a number.

Before you leave: a real walk, not a doorstep pee. Twenty minutes of sniffing tires a dog more than an hour of marching. Then leave something to do. A frozen stuffed toy buys an hour. A puzzle feeder, another chunk. A dog that sleeps through the middle of the day had a morning; a dog that stared at the wall had a sentence to serve.
Midday help changes everything: a dog walker, a neighbor kid, a lunchtime trip home. Even twice a week breaks the week open.
## What we watch for

At our office, dogs come to work with us, which is its own experiment. The thing we notice most is that tired dogs are calm dogs and busy-brained dogs are not. When we test a toy for the catalog, the question is never does the dog like it for five minutes. It is did the dog settle afterward. Products that wind a dog up fail. Products that give it a job pass.
If your days are long, do not feel guilty. Feel practical. Meet the needs at both ends, buy the middle hours something to do, and watch your own dog, not the poster.

posts.title: The daily walk matters more than you think
posts.excerpt: It is not exercise. It is the newspaper, the social club, and the therapy session, all in one.
body: A friend of mine has a big yard and a border collie, and for years he told himself the yard was enough. The dog had space. The dog ran around. Then the dog started barking at nothing, digging up the iris bed, and pacing at the window every afternoon at four.
The vet asked one question: how often do you walk him?
## The walk is not really about walking

To us, a walk is exercise. To a dog, it is the whole sensory world. Twenty minutes on a street is reading the paper, checking social media, hearing the gossip, and marking the neighborhood bulletin board, literally.

A yard is the same view every day. A walk is a changing feed. Dogs need novelty the way we need conversation, and sniffing is how they get it. Studies on scent work keep finding the same thing: dogs that are allowed to sniff freely on walks come home measurably calmer and more optimistic in how they approach new things.
## The shape of a good walk

Not every walk needs to be a march. Give the dog some decisions. Let it choose the route sometimes. Build in one sniff-spot where the leash goes loose and the nose goes down. Ten minutes of free sniffing beats forty minutes of heel at human pace.

The other half of the walk is yours. It is the one fixed ritual most dogs share with their person, the same time, the same streets, together. Dogs are routine animals, and routine shared with a favorite human reads as safety.
My friend started walking the collie twice a day, mostly to prove the vet wrong. The barking stopped in about two weeks. The iris bed recovered by spring.

When we talk to retail buyers about why a simple leash still sells year after year, this is the reason. Nothing fancy replaces the daily ritual. The walk is the product the dog is actually buying. The leash just comes with it.

posts.title: Old dogs, new homes: adopting a senior pet
posts.excerpt: You will get fewer years and better years. A case for the gray-muzzled dogs nobody picks first.
body: In most shelters, the oldest dogs are the last to leave. Puppies get adopted in days. A nine-year-old lab mix can wait months, watching every family walk past the kennel.
I understand why. Nobody wants to sign up for heartbreak on a schedule. But I want to make the case anyway, because the math people fear is not the math they get.
## What you actually sign up for

Yes, fewer years. What you get in exchange is a dog that is already finished being a project. House training, done. Chewed sofas, in the past. Basic manners, installed years ago by someone else's effort. A senior dog wants a soft bed, a short walk, and a person, in roughly that order.
The adjustment period is often shockingly short. Puppies need months of structure. Senior dogs frequently settle in a week, as if they know the assignment.
## The real costs, honestly

Vet bills are the honest downside. Bloodwork, dental care, arthritis management. Some senior dogs arrive with conditions that need daily medication. Ask the shelter what they know, get the first vet visit done early, and budget realistically.

Comfort gear matters more than training gear at this stage. An orthopedic bed is not a luxury for a dog with stiff hips, and ramps beat jumping. Non-slip floors are kindness. Warmth matters; old dogs feel cold first.

This is where our product decisions have shifted over the years. We used to make beds that photographed well. Now we make beds a twelve-year-old dog can get into without a running start, with a lip that is a help rather than a hurdle, and covers that survive being washed twice a week.

A senior adoption will end sooner than you want. Everything you love ends sooner than you want. What people who adopt old dogs tend to report is the same thing: the gratitude is different. Quieter, and somehow more obvious. The dog knows what a home is worth. It had one, it lost it, and now it has one again.

posts.title: Two cats or one? What we learned the hard way
posts.excerpt: Getting a second cat to fix a lonely first cat can backfire. Here is how to do it right, or decide not to.
body: The plan was simple. Our cat Nana worked long days alone at home with us, so we would get her a friend. Companion, entertainment, problem solved. We brought home a bouncy six-month-old and put him on the living room floor.
Nana looked at us like we had betrayed a treaty. Then she went under the bed for a month.
## Cats are not dogs about company

A dog hears second dog and thinks pack. A cat hears second cat and thinks competitor, at least at first. Cats are territorial by default. In their natural life, the cats they accept are family, and family is chosen slowly, on their terms.
So the honest answer to two cats or one is: it depends on the cats, not on the arithmetic of your guilt.
## When a second cat works well

Kittens raised together usually bond for life. Two adults introduced slowly can become genuine companions, especially if they are both youngish and laid back. The pairing that goes best is a confident resident cat with a calm newcomer of similar energy.
## The introduction nobody should skip

Separate rooms for the first days. Swap scents before faces: trade blankets, feed on opposite sides of a closed door. Then short, supervised meetings, ending on purpose before anything goes wrong. Weeks, not days. Rushing the introduction is the single most common mistake, and it is the one we made.
Resource math matters too. The rule is one litter box per cat plus one, and food and water stations in separate spots. Most cat conflict is really resource conflict wearing a fur coat.

Six months on, Nana and the kitten are not cuddly friends. They are colleagues. They share the sunny window in shifts, they play chase at 11pm, and Nana grooms his ears when she thinks nobody is watching. Would she have chosen this? Hard to say. Is the household better? Yes.
If you do it, do it slowly. If you decide against it, add a window perch and daily play instead. Cats are flexible about how their social needs get met. People are the ones who like tidy answers.

posts.title: Puppy chewing season: what actually worked
posts.excerpt: Teething is not a behavior problem. It is construction work. Manage the site and save your furniture.
body: Between four and seven months, our puppy destroyed: one slipper, two chair legs, a phone charger, the corner of a rug, and a hardcover novel, which he seemed to savor. This is not a cautionary tale. It is a season, and like weather, you prepare for it rather than resent it.
## Why puppies chew like it is their job

Because it is. Adult teeth coming in hurt, and chewing relieves the pressure. Then, right when teething ends, the real reason arrives: puppy adolescence meets the fact that puppies explore the world with their mouths. Chewing is also self-soothing, like nail-biting for a creature with no nails.
Punishing chewing teaches nothing useful. The drive is chemical. Your job is to give it a place to go.
## The three-part system that saved our sofa

One, rotation. Ten toys out is zero toys. We kept three or four available and swapped weekly so everything stayed interesting. Frozen was best on sore-gum days: a wet rope toy from the freezer, or a stuffed rubber toy frozen overnight.

Two, trade, never chase. Chasing a puppy with a slipper makes the slipper a prize. Trading for something better makes dropping things a habit. Our dog would eventually spit out contraband on sight, expecting an upgrade. That habit saved his life more than once, on street-floor findings.
Three, confinement you can trust. A pen or a puppy-proofed room when nobody could watch him. Management is not cheating; it is how the shoes survive long enough for the habit work to stick.
## A note from the product side

Chewing season is also how we test. A sample that survives a teething lab puppy for a month has earned its place in the catalog. Several of our toughest toy designs exist because of that one winter, chosen by a puppy who was extremely good at his job.
The season ends. The novel was replaced. The chair legs survived with minor scarring, and the dog, now grown, has not touched a slipper in years. Hang in there and hide the chargers.

posts.title: A quiet home is a happy home
posts.excerpt: Cats hear the world at volumes we do not. Small changes to your noise floor can change your cat.
body: People are usually surprised to learn that a cat's hearing runs roughly two octaves above ours. That vacuum you hate is worse for the cat. The TV you fell asleep to, the speaker on the fridge, the blender, the door slam. All of it arrives louder, and some of it arrives in ranges we simply cannot perceive.
## What noise does to a cat

Cats rarely show fear the way dogs do. What they show is avoidance. A cat living with constant background noise does not necessarily hide all day. It picks worse real estate: behind the sofa instead of the windowsill, under the bed instead of the middle of the room. Over time, a noisy home quietly shrinks a cat's map of it.

Loud sudden noise is worse than steady noise, and unpredictability is the worst of all. A cat can adapt to a city street outside the window. It never fully adapts to random explosions from the kitchen appliance.
## The cheap fixes

Give the cat one genuinely quiet room, or at least one quiet zone with covered escape routes. Put the litter box far from the laundry machines; imagine doing your business next to a jet engine. Run the loud appliances when the cat is out of the room or has somewhere high and enclosed to go. Rug and curtains do more than people expect; hard floors bounce sound around a room like a squash court.
Watch where the cat chooses to sleep. That spot is data about your home's acoustics from the resident expert.

This sensitivity shaped more of our product line than almost anything else. The quietest wheel on our cat tree samples, the felt pads under every platform, the decision to skip bells on most toys, all trace back to watching cats avoid the loud versions. A quiet product is a used product. The louder alternative ends up in a closet, and the cat ends up in the box it shipped in, which is at least silent.

posts.title: Road trips with your dog, minus the chaos
posts.excerpt: Six hours in a car with a dog can be a highlight of the year or a long argument. Preparation decides which.
body: Our first road trip with the dog was four hours of crossed fingers. He paced between seats, drooled on the console, and barked at a motorcycle once per hour, like a sad alarm. The second trip, a month later, was different, and the difference was almost entirely preparation.
## Before the trip
Short drives first. A dog that only ever rides to the vet learns that the car means the vet. Two-minute trips to nowhere that end in a walk or a game rewrite that association fast.

Book dog-friendly stays and confirm, twice. Check that your dog's microchip registration has your current phone number. Pack a real bag for the dog: food, bowl, water bottles, towel, leash, poop bags, a copy of vaccinations, and any medication plus one spare day of it.
## In the car

A dog loose in a cabin is a projectile in a hard brake and a distraction the rest of the time. A crash-tested harness clipped to the belt, or a secured carrier or barrier for smaller dogs, is the single upgrade that matters most. Seat covers save the interior; a familiar blanket saves the dog's nerves.
Stop every two to three hours. Water at every stop, a short walk, and no big meals right before driving, which is the main cure for drooling. Windows cracked for smell, never fully open at speed.
Never, ever leave a dog in a parked car in warm weather. The twenty-second version of this rule is: cars heat up in minutes even on mild days.
## At the destination

First hour sets the tone. Walk the dog on leash around the new place, let it sniff the room, put down water, set up its bed in a corner before anything else happens. A dog that has a den inside a strange place settles within the evening.
Keep feeding times identical to home. Keep one walk ritual identical too. Dogs do not need the vacation to be exciting. They need it to be familiar, in a different place.
By the third trip ours slept from the first minute of driving. Now the hard part of road trips is that the dog gets in the car every time we do, hopeful, for weeks afterward.

posts.title: Why cats knead (and why it means so much)
posts.excerpt: The biscuit-making is leftover kittenhood, and it is aimed at you for a reason.
body: Somewhere tonight, a cat is pressing its paws into a blanket, alternating left right left right, eyes half closed, completely absorbed. Biscuit making, kneading, making bread. Whatever your family calls it, it is one of the strangest and sweetest things cats do.
## Where it comes from

Kneading starts in the first days of life. Kittens push against their mother to bring milk down, and the motion gets wired to a feeling of total safety and fullness. Most cats carry the habit into adulthood, the way some people still fidget with a necklace when they are relaxed.
The usual theory holds that it simply feels good to keep doing. Comfort behavior. A ritual from a safe time, replayed in safe moments.
## Why they knead you

Because you are the safe moment. A cat kneading your lap is telling you where it has filed you, next to milk and warmth and the earliest good feelings it ever had. There is no higher review in the cat world.

Soft surfaces invite it too. That is why blankets, beds, and laundry piles get the treatment. Cats also have scent glands in their paw pads, so kneading leaves a quiet personal mark on a place or a person.
## The claws, gently

Yes, it hurts when the program includes claw deployment. Never punish it; the behavior is pure affection. Trim the nails on schedule and put a thick blanket over your lap when the biscuits start, and everybody wins.

You can tell a lot about a product by whether it gets kneaded. In our sample room, the fabrics that survive a week of biscuit testing are the ones that go into production. Loose weaves pull apart under kneading claws within days; a tight, dense knit takes it for years. Cats are brutally honest QA engineers.
So when your cat sets to work on you, slow and rhythmic and shameless, know what it is saying. It is saying you remind it of the very first safety it ever knew. Not bad for a Tuesday evening.

posts.title: The lazy owner's guide to keeping pets healthy
posts.excerpt: No spreadsheets, no supplements drawer. Five habits that do most of the work.
body: Some pet owners keep binders. Vaccination dates, weight charts, dental logs. I admire them the way I admire people who fold fitted sheets. For everyone else, here is the short list that genuinely does most of the work.
## One: the monthly once-over

Same day every month, two minutes, hands on the animal. Run your fingers down the body, check ears, look at teeth if tolerated, feel the paw pads. You are not hunting for disease. You are learning the baseline, so that anything new announces itself early. Vets find most serious things late because owners had no baseline to compare against.
## Two: weigh the food, do not scoop it

A measuring cup can be off by twenty percent, which is the difference between a fit dog and a chunky one over a year. A cheap kitchen scale and a sticky note with the daily number ends the guessing forever. This one habit adds more healthy years than any supplement on the market.
## Three: teeth by treat
Brushing is best and most people will not. Fine. Chews and kibble sized to scrub, plus a vet dental when the breath turns feral. Bad breath is a flag, not a fact of life.
## Four: movement on schedule
Dogs need the walk even in rain, cats need the ten-minute wand toy even when they ignore it the first minute. Put it in the calendar like medicine, because it is.
## Five: the annual visit, even when nothing is wrong

One visit a year buys baseline bloodwork and an early look at the things that are quiet until they are not. Cats especially are professional illness hiders; the annual exam is often the only way anything gets caught in time.

That is the whole system. None of it takes talent, all of it takes five minutes, and together it covers maybe eighty percent of what determines whether your pet is thriving. Save the binder for people who enjoy binders. Your dog would rather you spend that time on the couch with them.

posts.title: Reading your dog's tail: it's not always happiness
posts.excerpt: A wagging tail is a sign of arousal, not a smile. Learning the difference prevents a lot of misunderstandings.
body: The most dangerous myth in dog body language is that a wagging tail means a friendly dog. Bite reports are full of witnesses saying the dog was wagging. It probably was. Tails wag for many reasons, and only some of them are hello.
## A wag is motion, and motion means something is up
Tails wag when a dog is emotionally activated. The emotion could be joy. It could also be uncertainty, alertness, frustration, or conflict. Height of arousal, not valence, is what the wag measures.

So read the whole dog, then the tail. Loose body, soft mouth, wiggling hips, tail at mid height sweeping wide: genuine social joy. Stiff body, hard stare, tail high and ticking in small sharp movements: that is arousal too, and it is not an invitation.
## The details that matter
Height is status and confidence. A tail clamped low or tucked is fear, and a scared dog that feels cornered is where bites come from.
Speed and width are intensity. The famous helicopter wag, full circle, whole rear end involved, is about as friendly as dog language gets.

Asymmetry is real. Research found dogs wag with a right-side bias when they feel positive about something and drift left under stress. You do not need to study sides at the park. Just notice when the wag looks tight, high, or small. Those are the ones that ask for space.
## Teaching kids the honest version

The rule for children is simple and safer than the old one: before petting any dog, ask the person, then let the dog choose. Hand low, let the dog come to you. If the body is loose and the dog pushes in, pet it. If it is stiff or turns away, thank it for the answer and move on.

Dogs spend their lives being polite in a language we barely read. The tail is the loudest word in that language, and it has more meanings than hello. A few minutes of learning it buys a lifetime of better conversations, and keeps everybody's hands safe.

posts.title: Moving house with pets, without the drama
posts.excerpt: Moving day is the most disruptive thing that happens in a pet's year. A plan turns chaos into a long weekend.
body: We have moved twice with pets, and the second time went nothing like the first, because the first time we did everything wrong. Boxes appeared suddenly, strangers carried furniture through the house all day, the cat vanished, and the dog lost his mind at every trip to the truck.
From the pet's point of view, we had demolished our shared world in a single day.
## The week before

Cats read the house as territory, so let them read the packing. Boxes can stay out for a couple of weeks. Cats supervise, climb in, mark them with cheek rubs. By moving day the boxes are furniture, not invaders.
Keep routines identical while the boxes multiply. Same feeding times, same walk times. The routine is the signal that the world still works.

For the day itself, board the pets or give them one closed room with their bed, water, litter, and a note on the door. A pet underfoot among strangers with heavy furniture is how doors get left open. Lost-pet reports spike on moving days for exactly this reason.
## Arrival, in the right order

Set up one room completely first. Bed, bowls, litter, familiar smells, then bring the pet in and let it own that room while the rest of the house fills up. Cats especially need a base camp; let them expand territory at their own pace, over days, not hours.

Dogs do better with a long walk before the first session of unpacking, and their bed placed in a spot that mirrors the old house, if you can manage it. Feed on the old schedule from day one. New address, same laws of physics.
## The settling window

Expect two or three weird weeks. Cats may sleep more and eat less for a few days; that is normal. What is not normal is a cat not eating for over two days or a dog that cannot settle after a week, and that is vet territory.
Update the microchip registration the same week. It takes five minutes and it is the whole point of having a microchip.

The second move, done this way, was almost boring. The cat claimed the new windowsill by evening. The dog had a nap mid-afternoon like it was any Tuesday. Pets do not need the move to be painless. They need it to be legible.

posts.title: The slow blink: how cats say I love you
posts.excerpt: Cats have a phrase that means everything is fine and I trust you. You can say it back.
body: There is a piece of cat language so simple that most people learn it by accident and so useful that I want to teach it to everyone: the slow blink.

You have seen it. The cat looks at you, eyes soft, and closes them slowly, holds a beat, opens again. Not a stare. Not a squint. A deliberate, unhurried close and open, like a tiny curtain acknowledging an old friend.
## What it means

In cat, prolonged direct eye contact is a threat. Staring is what rivals do. So a cat that looks at you, deliberately relaxes its eyes, and closes them in your presence is saying: I could be on guard, and I am choosing not to be. Around you, my defenses are down.

Researchers tested this formally a few years ago. Cats shown a human slow blink were more likely to slow blink back and more likely to approach an extended hand afterward. The expression works across species lines. It is probably the only sentence you can say in cat.
## How to say it back

Catch a calm moment. Cat across the room, relaxed, looking your way. Soften your own face, look at it with half-lidded eyes, close them slowly, hold a second, open slowly. Then look away. The look-away matters; it proves the whole thing was friendly and there is no follow-up stare.

Do not lean in, do not reach. Just the blink, then break eye contact. Do it a few times over a few days and watch what happens. Many cats will blink back. Some will get up and come over, because you just told them, in their own grammar, that you are safe.
It sounds like nothing until it works on a cat that does not come to people. Then it feels like a key.

We have a resident office cat who supervises sample arrivals, and new visitors are always surprised when she walks over to them and not the person waving toys at her. The ones she picks are almost always the quiet ones who happened to slow blink without knowing why. Cats keep their own census, and the slow blink is how you get counted as a friend.

posts.title: Why dogs love predictability
posts.excerpt: Your dog cannot read a calendar, but it can read a pattern. Patterns are how a dog feels safe.
body: Our dog does not own a watch, yet at 5:50pm he appears in the kitchen with the confidence of a train conductor. Breakfast at seven, the walk at eight, the neighborhood patrol at six. If we break the pattern, we hear about it.
People joke that dogs are little clocks. What is actually happening is deeper and worth knowing: dogs build their sense of safety out of patterns, the way we build it out of promises kept.
## Security comes from the pattern, not the person standing next to it

A dog that knows what happens next does not have to monitor the world for surprises. Predictability lowers the background hum of vigilance. That is why a fixed feeding time calms a dog more than extra treats, and why the same walk route can be soothing in a way a new park is not.

Watch a dog in a chaotic household: it is either frazzled or flat. Watch a dog in a dull-but-steady routine: it is relaxed, and oddly, more playful when playtime comes, because it can fully commit to an activity it saw coming.
## Where flexibility fits in

This is not a case for boring your dog. Patterns are the skeleton; you hang variety on them. Keep the anchors fixed, meaning meals, walks, sleep, and your return, and vary the content inside them: new routes on weekends, new games, new people.

The times routines matter most are the transitions, which are the moments dogs find hardest. Your departure, your return, bedtime, mealtime. Make those four boring, consistent, and short. No farewell operas at the door, no wild hellos that teach the return is a national holiday. Calm in, calm out. The dog learns that every parting has a sequel.
A senior dog with a steady day is a calmer dog. An anxious dog with a steady day often becomes a different dog within weeks, no medication involved.

When owners ask us why the same simple products sell for years, this is a lot of the answer. The mat, the bowl, the leash by the door at the same hour. The gear is not the point. The ritual the gear enables is. Your dog does not want a more exciting life. It wants a life where it knows what happens next, mostly, and knows who is holding the schedule. That is you, and the trust that builds is the whole relationship.

posts.title: The case for the boring leash
posts.excerpt: Retractable, glowing, multi-tool leashes all have their fans. The plain flat leash quietly wins for most dogs.
body: Every year the pet market invents a new leash. Retractable ones, bungee ones, leashes with lights, with bottle openers, with more hardware than a sailboat. I have tested most of them, and I am here to defend the boring one: a flat nylon or leather leash, about a meter and a half, one clip, one loop.
## What the plain leash does better

Communication. Training lives in the slack. With a fixed-length leash, your dog learns where you are without checking, because the leash goes tight at the same distance every time. That consistency is why trainers reach for it first.

A retractable leash teaches the opposite. The length always changes, so there is nothing to learn, and the constant light tension actually trains dogs to pull. The lock button fails eventually, usually at the worst moment, and the thin cord is a hand-injury specialty.
## Safety in the details nobody photographs

The clip is the part that matters. A cheap snap that rusts or sticks is the failure point of the whole system. A solid swivel snap, checked now and then for wear, is unglamorous and essential. The stitching near the loop takes the most stress of any part; if you see fraying there, retire the leash the way you would retire a worn tire.

Width matters less than people think. A wider leash is not automatically stronger; a good 20-millimeter nylon with tight weave will outlive a fat, floppy one. For small dogs, lighter hardware is kinder to the neck than thick leather.
Reflective stitching is the one upgrade I would never skip for city dogs, because it costs nothing on the walk and can matter enormously on the one dark evening something goes wrong.

When we designed our standard leash at Poteho, we argued about adding features for weeks and ended up cutting all of them. What stayed: tight-weave webbing, bar-tack stitching at every stress point, a tested swivel snap, and a reflective line stitched flat so it cannot rub off. It is a boring leash on purpose. Boring, in this category, is what reliability looks like.

posts.title: Why your cat loves the box more than the toy inside
posts.excerpt: You spent money on the toy. The cat read the box and made a decision. Here is the science of the box.
body: Every cat owner has funded this experiment. The new toy arrives. The cat sniffs the toy, walks away, and is found sitting in the packaging like it just won a throne.
This is not ingratitude. It is physics, or close to it.
## What the box offers

A box is a hiding place with one door. Cats are ambush predators with the anxiety settings of prey animals, which is a strange combination that the box solves perfectly: the cat can watch the world while the world cannot watch the cat's back.

Security is the first answer. The second is temperature. Cardboard is a decent insulator, and cats spend most of the day inside their thermal comfort zone, which runs hotter than ours. A box in a sunny spot is a heated den with a view.
The third answer is stress. In a study on shelter cats, cats given a box adapted to a new environment measurably faster than cats without one. The box is not entertainment. It is anxiety management.
## The fake-box finding

The strangest part: cats also sit in the outline of a box. In a study where boxes were just tape squares on the floor, cats stepped in and settled anyway. An illusion of a boundary was enough. That tells you how deep the enclosed-space preference runs. It is not about the cardboard. It is about the edges.
## What to do with this knowledge

Keep one box in circulation, rotated when it gets flattened. Put a soft pad in it. And if you are shopping for cat furniture, buy the principle, not the product: whatever you choose should offer enclosure and a clear vantage, or it will lose to the Amazon box forever.

That finding runs through our whole cat line. Enclosed beds outsell open mats in every market we ship to, and the design brief for our covered beds started with an actual shipping box in the sample room that three cats refused to give back. We are not embarrassed about it. We hired the box as a consultant, and it was excellent.

posts.title: A dog's senior years: what changes and what doesn't
posts.excerpt: The gray muzzle shows up around year seven. Most of what follows is manageable, and some of it is the best time you will have.
body: Nobody warns you that the first sign of your dog aging is usually the muzzle going gray, and that it shows up around year seven, right about when you finally feel like you have this dog thing figured out.
Aging is not a diagnosis. It is a set of slow changes, and almost all of them can be made easier.
## What changes

Joints first, usually. The dog that launched off the sofa starts taking the dismount in stages. Stiffness after long naps, slower on stairs, hesitating at the car. Arthritis is nearly universal in senior dogs and very treatable, so mention it early rather than accepting it as normal.

Sleep deepens and stretches. Senses dim gradually; many older dogs lose some hearing, and night vision fades. House rules may need small edits: lights left on in the hallway, mats on slippery floors, water bowls duplicated in more rooms.
Weight creeps up as metabolism slows, and it matters more now than ever, because extra kilograms ride directly on those aging joints.
## What does not change

The need for a job and a routine. Senior dogs still want the walk, even if it is the short loop at smell-pace. They still want to be included. What we call spoiling, longer sniff breaks, the good spot on the couch, is actually just correct scheduling for the stage they are in.
The love, obviously, does not change. If anything it gets quieter and more direct. A young dog loves you with its whole body. An old dog loves you with its eyes, from the bed, while you make coffee.
## Small upgrades that earn their cost

An orthopedic bed is the one purchase that changes daily life most; good foam keeps pressure off hips that now complain at dawn. Ramps for the car and the sofa prevent the jumps that cost them later. Raised bowls help some dogs with stiff necks. Twice-yearly vet visits instead of one, because senior things move faster.

We redesigned our whole bed line around this stage a few years back, after watching our own dog struggle to stand from a bed with tall sides. The new ones have a lower entry, real support foam, and a washable cover, because senior dogs and senior bladders are a package deal.

The senior years are not the sad epilogue people expect. Done thoughtfully, they are the years when the relationship is most settled, most wordless, and most mutually understood. Slower walks. Same dog. More gratitude per step.

posts.title: Heat safety for pets: the talk we have every summer
posts.excerpt: Every summer the same accidents happen. A short list that prevents nearly all of them.
body: Every summer, without fail, the same preventable things happen. The dog in the parked car. The shortened walk at noon. The bulldog who was fine right up until he was not. So this is the talk, the one we give customers, friends, and occasionally strangers in parking lots.
## The car, once and forever

A parked car is an oven on a timer. On a 24-degree day, the inside of a car can pass 38 degrees within ten minutes. Cracked windows change almost nothing. There is no safe duration, no shade, no quick errand. The dog stays home. That is the whole rule and it has no exceptions.
## Walking in heat

Try the pavement test with the back of your hand: seven seconds on the asphalt. If you cannot hold it, it burns paw pads. Early morning and late evening are the walking windows in summer; midday walks are for January.

Brachycephalic breeds, meaning the flat-faced crew like bulldogs, pugs, and Persians on the cat side, overheat at temperatures other dogs shrug off. So do overweight dogs, seniors, and thick-coated breeds. For them, summer walks are shorter, slower, and earlier than your schedule prefers. Their cooling system is simply built with a narrower margin.

Know the emergency signs: heavy panting that turns weak, bright red gums, wobbliness, vomiting, collapse. That is heatstroke, and it is a straight-to-vet emergency. Cool with lukewarm water and air on the way; ice-cold makes it worse.
## Water and the small stuff

Multiple water stations, refreshed daily, because stagnant warm water goes undrunk. Shade in the yard, always. A paddling pool is genuine equipment, not a photo prop. And grooming matters: a matted coat traps heat against the skin. Keep double-coated breeds brushed and never shaved to the skin; the coat insulates against heat too.

One product note we repeat every summer: cooling mats and elevated beds genuinely help, but only if the animal chooses to use them. Place them where the pet already naps, not where they photograph well. In our test homes, the elevated cots in the shade got used daily; the fancy ones in the sun got ignored all season. Location beats technology, as usual.

posts.title: How a pet changes your mornings
posts.excerpt: Before the alarm, there is a paw. Some thoughts on the least private wake-up service in the world.
body: There are people who wake up slowly, to sunlight and a moment of quiet reflection. I used to be one of them. Now I wake at 6:31 to a dog standing on my chest, breathing into my face with the urgency of a smoke alarm that loves me.
Owning a pet rewrites your mornings completely, and after years of this I have come to believe the rewrite is mostly an upgrade.
## The new schedule

Pets do not respect weekends. The cat's breakfast is at six, weekdays and Sundays alike, and the dog's internal clock has an error margin of about four minutes. You will become a morning person or a very good negotiator. Most people become a morning person, grudgingly, then genuinely.

There is worse company to keep. The morning now includes a walk before screens, which is the habit every wellness book sells and every dog delivers for free. Cold air, quiet streets, a dog completely thrilled to be alive at an hour when you were previously a zombie. It is difficult to stay completely grim while holding a leash attached to that much optimism.
## The small rituals

The cat's supervision of tooth-brushing. The dog's opinion of the coffee machine, which has been negative for six years and shows no signs of softening. The way both animals migrate to whichever corner of the kitchen the sun reaches first, like clockwork, while you make breakfast.

None of this shows up in the reasons people give for wanting a pet. Everyone says companionship, and they are right, but the daily texture of that companionship is oddly specific. It is mostly mornings. The evenings are for the couch; the mornings are for the contract.

There is research suggesting pet owners start the day with lower stress than non-owners, which my dog produced by standing on my bladder, but the finding holds. A creature that needs you before you have decided to need anything gets you moving, outdoors, on a rhythm.
I still have slow Sunday mornings sometimes, when the family is away and the pets are boarding. I sleep until nine. I do not like it. The 6:31 face is better.

posts.title: Grooming at home without either of you hating it
posts.excerpt: Five minutes often beats the monthly wrestling match. Building a grooming habit the gentle way.
body: Most home grooming fails for the same reason most New Year gym plans fail: it is designed as an event instead of a habit. The monthly full groom, tools laid out, towel on the floor, animal already suspicious. Everyone hates it by February.
The version that works is smaller and stranger: tiny sessions, high frequency, no agenda.
## The habit version

Start with thirty seconds of brushing while the pet is already relaxed, maybe after dinner. No restraint, no completion goal. You are not grooming; you are depositing good associations. Weeks of this, and the brush becomes a signal for calm.

Then stretch slowly. A minute. Two. Stop before your pet wants to stop, every time. The counterintuitive rule of animal training applies here in full: always end one minute before things go wrong, and the next session starts better than the last.
## The order that keeps peace

Body before face, always. Feet last, because feet are where trust runs out. Handle paws separately, casually, on their own days, pairing each touch with something good. Nail trims are the final boss and deserve their own campaign: one paw, one nail, treat, done, another day.

Brush choice does half the work. Short coats want rubber curry or bristle; long coats want a wide comb to break tangles before any brush touches them. Matting behind ears, under the collar line, and in the armpits is where problems start, so those three spots get checked weekly.

Baths: rare, lukewarm, and with dog or cat shampoo only. Human shampoo is the wrong pH and ruins the coat's skin barrier. A dirty coat brushes out easier after a bath, but a matted one does not, so demat comes first or you are just making felt.
## The quiet payoff

The point of all this is not the coat. It is that your hands on the animal become routine and neutral, which makes every future vet visit, pill, and emergency check easier. Grooming is trust maintenance disguised as coat maintenance.

When people ask why our grooming tools look plain, this is why. A slicker brush that does its job without yanking, a comb with rounded teeth, a nail clipper with a guard. Nobody needs seven tools. They need three boring ones and five calm minutes, most days of the week.

posts.title: What dogs hear when you talk to them
posts.excerpt: Your dog will never understand sentences, and understands far more than sentences anyway.
body: Talk to a dog long enough and you start to wonder what is actually getting through. The answer from research is delightfully lopsided: far fewer words than we imagine, and far more than the words.
## The words part

A trained pet dog reliably knows a handful of words; exceptional ones, like the border collie Chaser, learned over a thousand object names. But your average dog's vocabulary sits somewhere between twenty and a hundred, and most of it is proper nouns of their life: walk, dinner, the names of family members, the forbidden shoe.

Here is the part most owners miss: dogs do not parse grammar. Sit down, sit here, would you sit, sit, and down, all collapse into whichever sound pattern they have learned to bet on. Consistency of sound beats correctness of grammar every time. A dog trained on a word in one language will ignore your flawless translation of it.
## The everything-else part

The bigger channel is not the words. Tone carries first: dogs separate cheerful from neutral from low and serious without any training at all. Brain imaging work found that dogs process familiar words and emotional tone in separate hemispheres, and they combine the two. Meaning arrives as tone plus word, and mismatches confuse them. A bright voice saying bad dog produces a visibly torn animal.
Around the voice sits everything else: your posture, your pace, the smell of stress, the length of your sigh. Anyone who has tried to fake cheerfulness at a nervous dog knows the audit runs deep.
## What to actually do

Pick one sound per concept, short and distinct, and defend it like a password. Keep your tone matched to your meaning. Talk as much as you like; dogs appear to enjoy the channel being open even when the content is beyond them. Narrating your day to a dog is a fine thing to do, and there is no evidence it hurts, and much that the dog likes the ritual of it.

The famous finding that dogs process speech asymmetrically, familiar words to one ear, emotional charge to the other, matches what owners have always sensed. The dog is not listening to your sentences. It is listening to you. The sentence just rides along.

posts.title: The 3pm zoomies, explained
posts.excerpt: Flat out laps around the house at top speed, for no visible reason. There are actually several reasons.
body: The technical name is Frenetic Random Activity Periods, which scientists clearly named while laughing. You know it as the zoomies: the sudden full-speed gallop, tight corners, low slung turns, sometimes with a toy, sometimes with nothing but pure velocity.
Cats do the 3am version. Dogs do it after baths, at dusk, at the park gate, and, with great reliability, at around three in the afternoon.
## What zoomies actually are
Energy discharge, mostly. A body that has been storing energy, from rest, excitement, or relief, hits a threshold and dumps it all at once. The zoomies are less a decision than a pressure valve.

Watch when they happen and the pattern makes sense. After a bath: relief and the weird sensation of being suddenly lighter. After a long day of being polite: the accumulated arousal of self-control finding an exit. Morning and evening zoomies track the natural activity peaks of a crepuscular species, the dawn-and-dusk schedule written into dogs and cats long before sofas existed.

Stress can also trigger them. A dog that zooms when guests arrive may be discharging nerves, not joy. Context tells you which. Loose body, play bows, happy face: fun. Wide eyes, frantic pacing before the run: that is anxiety looking for a door.
## Should you do anything

Usually, no. Zoomies are normal, healthy, and self-limiting. The jobs of the owner are simply these: clear the runway, meaning nothing breakable or slippery on the route, and let it end on its own. Do not chase a zooming dog in a park; you will not win, and being chased reads as the best game ever invented.

If the zoomies are constant, that is information too. It usually means the dog's day is missing structured exercise or work, so the pressure valve opens hourly. More walk, more sniffing, a training session, and the eruption schedule calms down.

There is no product that replaces a zoomie, and we have never tried to make one. The closest we came was watching which toy a dog grabs before starting its lap. It is almost always the one it can carry at full speed, which is why our rope toys are sized for a sprinting jaw and not for the shelf. The zoomie picks the inventory.

posts.title: Introducing a new pet to the family (slowly)
posts.excerpt: Whether it is a second dog, a cat into a dog house, or a kitten into a cat kingdom, the rule is the same: weeks, not hours.
body: The movies have lied to us about this for a hundred years. In the film, the new puppy and the old dog sniff once, chase each other around a tree, and are friends for life by the fade-out. In real houses, the fade-out takes three to eight weeks, and the speed at which you go is the single biggest factor in whether it works.
## The principle

Your resident pet did not agree to this. From its point of view, a stranger has arrived claiming resources it spent years securing. The goal of every good introduction is to make the stranger boring before it makes it close. Fear fades with repetition; that is the entire trick, and there is no shortcut around it.
## Dog to dog

First meeting on neutral ground, a park neither dog considers home, both on loose leashes, walks parallel with distance. Let them arc past each other a few times over days. Home meetings come after, in the yard if there is one, short and calm, ending before anyone gets stiff or pushy. Feed separately, always, forever if needed. Resource guarders exist, and food is the usual court.

Supervise everything for the first weeks. Separate when you leave the house. Give the resident dog its own retreat, and honor it. The most common mistake is lavishing attention on the newcomer to reassure ourselves. Reassure the resident instead.
## Cat into a dog household, or the reverse

This one runs on geography more than friendship. The cat needs vertical space the dog cannot reach, and every early meeting happens with the cat above the dog's nose or behind a barrier. Baby gates are the best invention this process has. Scent goes first, traded blankets, meals on opposite sides of a door. Face-to-face comes weeks later, dog on leash, calm, brief, and rewarded.
Some pairs become friends. Many become tolerant colleagues. A few will always need management. All three outcomes are successes if nobody is stressed.
## The honest expectations

Watch for the good signs: parallel napping, play with role swaps, relaxed eating in shared space. Watch for the bad ones: the resident pet eating less, hiding more, or guarding spots it never guarded. Those mean slow down, not give up.
Time does the rest. The introduction is not an event you attend. It is a season you get through, and the reward for going slowly is a household that settles for good.

posts.title: Travel with cats: easier than you think
posts.excerpt: Cats travel badly when the plan is bad. With a plan, they are surprisingly portable.
body: Cats have a reputation as terrible travelers, and it is deserved, in the same way a person would be a terrible traveler if every journey of their life went straight to the dentist.
Fix what the journey means, and most cats handle travel better than their owners do.
## Weeks before

The carrier comes out of storage and becomes living room furniture. Feeding near it, treats in it, the door removed if it has one. A cat that naps in its carrier on ordinary Tuesdays has already won half the trip.
Do a rehearsal drive: five minutes, no destination, home again, treat. Then ten. The car stops predicting the vet.

If your cat is truly anxious, talk to the vet about it in advance. There are legitimate options, and the right one depends on the cat and the length of the trip. Do not improvise with human medication.
## The day of

Feed light, hours before. Line the carrier with something that smells like the cat's usual spot, and bring a spare pad, because accidents happen on long days. Cover the carrier with a thin blanket once in the car; darkness settles most cats faster than anything else you can do.
Secure the carrier on the floor behind a seat or belted in, never loose on a seat and never in a cargo area. A frightened cat inside a loose carrier during a hard brake is the scenario to avoid.
For road trips, keep the carrier closed at stops. The classic lost-cat-at-the-gas-station story begins with an open door and a confident prediction that the cat would not dare. It dares.
## Arriving somewhere that is not home

Set up one closed room first: litter, water, the carrier left open as a den, familiar blanket. Let the cat decompress there while the rest of the space settles. Most cats expand their territory within a day or two if the base camp felt safe.
And update the microchip details before any big move or trip. It costs nothing and it is the difference between a story with a bad afternoon in it and a story with a bad ending.

Our most-traveled office cat logs a few hundred kilometers a year between our sample rooms, asleep in the same worn carrier the whole way. She is not a brave cat. She is a well-briefed one. That is the entire difference, and it is available to any cat with a patient human and a carrier that means good news.

posts.title: Six years of making pet products: what we've learned
posts.excerpt: We started Poteho in 2020 with a simple idea and a small sample room. Some notes from six years of shipping pet products.
body: In 2020, in the middle of a year that made everyone reconsider their plans, we started Poteho. The idea was not complicated: make pet products we would actually use with our own animals, and treat the shops and brands that sell them the way we would want to be treated.
Six years on, we ship to retailers across more than thirty countries. Along the way we learned some things the easy way and more things the hard way. Here are the ones worth writing down.
## The animal is the customer

Our sample room has hosted every kind of tester: office dogs on payroll, resident cats with strong opinions, and a rotating cast of neighbor pets. The pattern never broke. Products designed to impress a buyer photograph well; products designed for the animal get reordered. A bed is not bought twice because it looked good in the showroom. It is bought again because a dog slept on it for four years and the store got asked for the name.
## Boring usually wins

The zippers that never jam, the stitching at every stress point, the swivel clips that survive salt air and -10 degree mornings. Nobody writes reviews praising a buckle that worked for five years, and that is exactly the point. Most of good product design is the absence of complaints.
## Small orders deserve real attention

We started small ourselves, so we never built the business around minimums that crush a first-time shop. A store testing fifty units is not a lesser customer than a chain ordering ten thousand. Every big account we have today started as someone's careful little test order.
## Pets are family, in the data and in person

The pet market grew through these six years while other categories wobbled, and the reason is visible in every order: people stopped thinking of food and gear as expenses and started thinking of them as part of the household budget, right next to the kids' shoes. We see it in what sells, and we live it at home like everyone else.
## What has not changed
We still test everything on our own animals before it ships. We still answer emails like a small company, because the day we stop is the day we become something else.

To the shops, the brands, and the pet parents who trusted a young company over the last six years: thank you. Milo the office cat, who has approved every catalog since 2020, would say the same, but she is on the warmest sample bed in the building and will not be disturbed.
